passages.t: Carried to Jerusalem, and the idol of jealousy
passages.happening:
In the sixth year, Ezekiel is sitting in his house with the elders of Judah before him when the hand of the Lord GOD falls on him (verse 1). A figure of fire and brightness takes him by the hair, and the Spirit carries him ‘in visions of God to Jerusalem’ (verse 3), to the north gate of the inner court, where ‘the idol that provokes jealousy was seated’ (verse 3). There too is the glory of the God of Israel (verse 4).

God asks whether Ezekiel sees the great abominations the house of Israel is committing ‘to drive Me far from My sanctuary’ (verse 6), and he adds that Ezekiel will see worse.
passages.hearers:
The date is late summer or early autumn of 592 BC. Jerusalem still stood under Zedekiah. The elders in Ezekiel's house were leaders of the exiles who came to him for a word from God.

The trip is a vision. Ezekiel's body stays in Babylon, but he is shown what is happening in the temple. An idol that provokes jealousy means an image that rouses God's jealous love, the love of a husband who will not share his bride. Its place at the north gate, at the very entrance to the inner court, shows how far things had gone.
passages.later: Manasseh had once set a carved Asherah pole in the temple (2 Kings 21:7). The law calls the LORD ‘a jealous God’ (Exodus 20:5).
passages.asks: The idol stood at the very entrance to God's house. Ask what you have allowed to stand at the doorway of your worship. And ask what it would take to remove it.

passages.happening:
God shows Ezekiel a hole in the wall and tells him to dig through it. Inside, every kind of crawling creature and unclean beast is carved around the walls, with the idols of Israel (verses 7-10). Seventy elders stand there with censers, and among them ‘Jaazaniah son of Shaphan’ (verse 11). They say, ‘The LORD does not see us; the LORD has forsaken the land’ (verse 12).

At the north gate, women sit ‘weeping for Tammuz’ (verse 14). In the inner court, between the porch and the altar, about twenty-five men turn their backs on the temple and bow to the east ‘in worship of the sun’ (verse 16). The land is full of violence (verse 17). So God says he will act in wrath and will not listen to their loud cries (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
Each scene is a real form of ancient worship. The carved animals suggest the kind of imagery found in Egyptian religion, and the secret room a private cult among the ruling class. Tammuz was a Mesopotamian god whose death was mourned in ritual lament; a month of the Babylonian calendar, later of the Jewish calendar, bears his name. Sun worship was widespread, and a generation earlier Josiah had removed horses dedicated to the sun from the temple entrance.

The twenty-five men face east with their backs to the temple, a picture of turning away from God in his own house.

A royal secretary named Shaphan brought King Josiah the book of the law, and his sons later protected Jeremiah. If this Jaazaniah belonged to that family, as many scholars think, the scene is especially bitter, though the text does not say so.
passages.later: Josiah ‘removed from the entrance to the house of the LORD the horses that the kings of Judah had dedicated to the sun’ (2 Kings 23:11). The psalm describes the wicked who say, ‘The LORD does not see’ (Psalm 94:7).
passages.hard:
How could religious leaders practice idolatry inside the temple and still think of themselves as faithful?

Verse 12 gives a clue. The elders believed that the LORD did not see them and had forsaken the land. After the deportation of 597 BC, many in Jerusalem may have decided that the God of Israel had failed or withdrawn, and turned to other powers for help while keeping the outward forms of temple life. Ancient religion was also generally inclusive; adding one more god did not feel like betrayal to most people. The prophets insisted that the LORD is not one god among many but the only God, and that his covenant with Israel was exclusive. The chapter shows that religious practice can go on at full volume while real trust has moved somewhere else.
passages.asks: The elders kept the forms of worship while trusting other powers. Ask where your outward faith and your real trust have come apart. And ask what you do in the dark that you would not do in the light.
